To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) greater birth weight was associated in adulthood with greater lean mass, but lower fat mass, 2) weight gain from birth to 2 years was associated with greater lean mass and lower fat mass, whereas weight gain from 2 to 20 years was associated with higher fat mass, and 3) height gain from birth to age 20 years was not associated with fat mass but was associated with higher levels of lean mass and lower levels of adiposity.

higher birth weight and greater infant weight gain are associated with higher lean and lower android/gynyoid ratios in old age, whereas greater weight gains in later childhood and early adolescence are associated with higher fat mass and fat/lean ratio.
greater weight gain in early life may be beneficial for lean mass and lower fat mass, but greater weight gain in late childhood and adolescence may increase fat mass and android/gynid ratio.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between early growth and the development of obesity and its consequences in adulthood.
the relationship between early growth and body fatness in later life and whether there are gender differences in the relationship.
the relationship between birth weight and weight change in childhood and the risk of obesity in adulthood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a high birth weight, and greater weight gain before birth, and in infancy, are associated with a greater lean mass and lower body fat in later life.
the more a person grows in early life, the more they will grow in later life.
the more weight gained in early life the better, but this is only true up to the point where it is no longer associated with higher lean and lower fat mass.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the greater the weight gain in infancy and childhood, the greater the fat mass in later life.
higher birth weight and greater early weight gain may be beneficial for lean mass, whereas higher weight gain in later life may be detrimental for fat and lean mass and fat/lean ratio.
greater weight gain in early life may be beneficial, whereas greater weight and height gains in later life may be detrimental.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the timing of weight gain matters.
greater growth in early life (before birth, infancy and early childhood) may be beneficial for fat and lean mass later in life.
the associations between birth weight and growth in infancy and fat and lean mass later in life are not as straightforward as previously thought.
